newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Optus continues funding ARL beyond '99.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Optus continues funding ARL beyond '99.

text.p: Australian telecommunications group Optus Communications said on Friday its Optus Vision pay television unit would continue its funding arrangements with the Australian Rugby League (ARL) for 1998, 1999 and beyond.
"The funding package is in line with the commitment Optus made to the ARL and its clubs last year," Optus chief executive Peter Howell-Davies said in a statement.
The statement did not specify how much the funding arrangements would be for.
Optus is thought to have provided over A$120 million in the two years the ARL has battled for control of the game with the rival Super League competition of media mogul Rupert Murdoch's News Corp.
Optus is paying each of the ARL's 12 teams A$1.8 million in 1997 and also shows ARL matches on its pay television station.
Murdoch's Foxtel pay-TV has Super League, while Australia's richest man, Kerry Packer, once a staunch ARL backer, struck a deal with Murdoch in January.
Packer now has terrestrial rights for both leagues and talk of a compromise between the warring camp has been rife for the past two months.
Optus, who had said it would agree to back a separate 1998 competition if necessary, said in Friday's statement it would support a merged competition.
"Optus is resolute in its support for a merged competition -- there can be no doubt that a single competition is what is best for the game of rugby league," Howell-Davies said.
Howell-Davies said its relationship with the ARL continued to make sense commercially.
"Our sponsorship of the Optus Cup and the pay television rights to the ARL are providing outstanding benefits to our business," he said.
ARL Chief Executive Neil Whittaker said all 12 clubs in the competition had individually confirmed their written commitments to remain with the ARL.
Whittaker and Optus Communications Marketing Director Russell Scrimshaw told a news conference they could not divulge the details of the reaffirmed funding agreement.

Speculation has grown in recent weeks that Optus may withdraw its funding of the ARL and its clubs in the wake of a change of ownership at Optus and as moves to rationalise the loss-making pay television industry have gathered pace.
Cable & Wireless Plc increased its stake in Optus to 49 percent from 24.5 percent on July 1 and one of its executives, Howell-Davies, took over the chief executives role at Optus.
"It's an opportunity to say with new shareholders and a new shareholding structure that the arrangement hasn't changed and it's continuing as before," Scrimshaw said.
Mayne Nickless Ltd is the other major shareholder in Optus, with 24.9 percent of Optus.

A resolution of the expensive battle between News and Telstra's Foxtel cable television service and Optus Vision is seen a crucial factor in the success of floats of Telstra and Optus planned for later this year and next year respectively.
